summary.text: Memorylessness is a property of some probability distributions: past failures or elapsed time do not affect future trials or further wait time.
Only two distributions have it: the geometric in the discrete case and the exponential in the continuous case.
It models the number of coin flips until landing heads and the time between two earthquakes.

items.prompt: You flip a fair coin and get five tails in a row. In a memoryless model of flips until heads, what does that history do to the next flip?

It makes heads more likely next
It makes heads less likely next

items.explain: Memorylessness means the number of previous failed trials has no effect on future trials.

items.prompt: Someone says a long quiet stretch without an earthquake makes one more likely soon. Under a memoryless model of time between earthquakes, what is true?

options.label: The elapsed time raises the chance of one
The elapsed time lowers the chance of one

items.explain: If a continuous distribution is memoryless, it must be the exponential distribution.

items.prompt: Which statement best captures what memorylessness means?

options.label: The wait so far changes nothing about the wait still to come
The longer you wait, the sooner the event must arrive
Each wait must be exactly as long as the one before
The event can only occur once during the wait

items.explain: It describes situations where elapsed time or previous failures do not affect future trials or further wait time.

paragraphs.heading: A distribution that forgets
paragraphs.text: Memorylessness is a property that some probability distributions have. It describes a kind of waiting or trying in which the past makes no difference. However many failures you have already seen, or however long you have already waited, the future trials and the wait still ahead are unaffected. Put plainly, the count of earlier failed attempts, or the time already gone by, is independent of what comes next.

paragraphs.heading: Only two distributions qualify
paragraphs.text: Just two distributions have this property: the geometric distribution and the exponential distribution. The geometric one is the memoryless choice in discrete settings, and the exponential one is the memoryless choice in continuous settings. Each is the only one of its kind. If a discrete distribution is memoryless, it has to be geometric, and if a continuous distribution is memoryless, it has to be exponential.

paragraphs.heading: Coin flips and earthquakes
paragraphs.text: In the discrete case, picture an endless run of trials, each independent of the others and all following the same chances, known as Bernoulli trials. The question is when the first success arrives. Counting how many times you toss a coin before it lands heads is the everyday example. In the continuous case, memorylessness is used to model random happenings such as the gap in time between one earthquake and the next.

paragraphs.heading: Why the continuous case is exponential
paragraphs.text: The reasoning that pins down the continuous case works with the survival function, written S(t). Shrinking the input of the survival function by a factor k and taking a k-th root gives S(t/k) = S(t)^(1/k). That equality holds for any rational number standing in for k. Since S is continuous and there is always a rational number as close as you like to any real number, it then holds for every real number as well.

paragraphs.heading: Where the formula lands
paragraphs.text: Following this through gives S(t) = e^(−λt), where λ = −ln S(1) is zero or more. That is exactly the survival function of the exponential distribution. So a continuous distribution that forgets its past has no other shape it can take. The discrete story ends the same way, with the geometric distribution as the only possible answer.
